glossary.Multifactorial: Caused by many factors acting together rather than one single cause.
glossary.Hyperkalaemia: High blood potassium, which can cause dangerous heart rhythms.
glossary.Renal bruit: A whooshing sound heard over the abdomen or flank from turbulent flow in a narrowed renal artery.
glossary.Abdominal bruit: A whooshing sound heard with a stethoscope over the abdomen, from turbulent blood flow in a narrowed artery.
glossary.CKD: Chronic kidney disease: long-term loss of kidney function over months to years.
glossary.AKI: Acute kidney injury: a sudden fall in kidney function over hours to days.
glossary.Bilateral idiopathic adrenal hyperplasia: Enlargement of both adrenal glands for no known reason; the commonest cause of primary hyperaldosteronism.
glossary.Palpitations: An unpleasant awareness of your own heartbeat.
glossary.Tachycardia: Heart rate above 100 beats per minute.
glossary.Café-au-lait spots: Flat, light-brown skin patches; many of them suggest neurofibromatosis type 1.
glossary.Neurofibromas: Benign soft lumps growing from nerve sheaths, typical of neurofibromatosis type 1.
glossary.Medullary thyroid carcinoma: Thyroid cancer of the calcitonin-making C cells, seen in MEN2.
glossary.Cushing's syndrome: Illness caused by long-term excess cortisol, with weight gain, high BP and high glucose.
glossary.Steroids: Corticosteroid drugs such as prednisolone, which can raise BP.
glossary.Encephalopathy: Diffuse brain dysfunction causing confusion, drowsiness or seizures.
glossary.ICP: Intracranial pressure: the pressure inside the skull.
glossary.Aortic dissection: A tear in the aortic wall letting blood split its layers; a surgical emergency.
glossary.Stroke: Sudden loss of brain function from a blocked or bleeding brain artery.
glossary.Heart failure: The heart cannot pump enough blood to meet the body's needs.
glossary.FBC: Full blood count: haemoglobin, white cells and platelets.
glossary.U&Es: Urea and electrolytes: blood test of kidney function, sodium and potassium.
glossary.Urinalysis: Testing urine, usually with a dipstick, for blood, protein, glucose and more.
glossary.Urine dipstick: A strip dipped in urine that changes colour to show blood, protein or glucose.
glossary.ECG: Electrocardiogram: a recording of the heart's electrical activity.
glossary.Plasma free metanephrines: Blood test for breakdown products of adrenaline and noradrenaline; the first test for phaeochromocytoma.
glossary.Fractionated metanephrines: Separate measurements of metanephrine and normetanephrine, here collected in urine over 24 hours.
glossary.Tumour localisation: Imaging to find exactly where a tumour sits once blood tests suggest it is there.
glossary.High-resolution CT: A CT scan with thin slices that shows fine detail.
glossary.Ramipril: An ACE inhibitor used for hypertension, heart failure and after MI.
glossary.Lisinopril: An ACE inhibitor used for hypertension and heart failure.
glossary.Losartan: An angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB), used when ACE inhibitors cause cough.
glossary.Aortic stenosis: Narrowing of the aortic valve, which blocks blood leaving the left ventricle.
glossary.Dry cough: A cough with no phlegm; a classic side effect of ACE inhibitors.
glossary.Amlodipine: A calcium channel blocker that relaxes arteries to lower BP.
glossary.Nifedipine: A calcium channel blocker used for hypertension, including in pregnancy.
glossary.Ankle oedema: Swelling of the ankles from fluid; a common side effect of calcium channel blockers.
glossary.Gum hypertrophy: Overgrowth of the gums, a side effect of calcium channel blockers.
glossary.Reflex tachycardia: A fast heart rate triggered as the body responds to a sudden drop in BP.
glossary.Thiazide-like diuretic: A water tablet acting on the distal tubule that lowers BP, such as indapamide.
glossary.Bendroflumethiazide: A thiazide diuretic, now second choice to indapamide for hypertension.
glossary.Gout: Painful joint inflammation caused by urate crystals.
glossary.Erectile dysfunction: Difficulty getting or keeping an erection.
glossary.Atorvastatin: A statin drug that lowers cholesterol to cut cardiovascular risk.
glossary.Verapamil: A rate-slowing calcium channel blocker that weakens heart contraction; avoid in heart failure.
glossary.Pulmonary oedema: Fluid in the lungs' air spaces, causing breathlessness.
glossary.Prediabetes: Blood glucose higher than normal but below the diabetes threshold.
glossary.Secondary prevention: Treatment to stop a disease or event coming back or getting worse once it has happened.
glossary.Beta-blocker: Drug that blocks adrenaline's beta receptors, slowing the heart and lowering BP.
glossary.Atenolol: A beta-blocker; side effects include lethargy and erectile dysfunction.
glossary.Alpha-1 blocker: Drug that relaxes blood vessels by blocking alpha-1 adrenergic receptors.
glossary.Doxazosin: An alpha-1 blocker used for resistant hypertension and enlarged prostate.
glossary.Angioplasty: Widening a narrowed artery with a balloon passed through a catheter.
glossary.Stenting: Placing a small mesh tube in an artery to hold it open.
glossary.Sympathetic activity: Output of the 'fight or flight' nervous system, which raises heart rate and tightens vessels.
glossary.Peripheral vascular resistance: The resistance to blood flow from the small arteries; when it rises, BP rises.
glossary.Renal perfusion pressure: The pressure driving blood through the kidneys.
glossary.Renin: Enzyme released by the kidney when its blood flow falls, starting the RAAS.
glossary.Angiotensin I: An inactive hormone made by renin; ACE turns it into angiotensin II.
glossary.Angiotensin II: A hormone that tightens blood vessels and triggers aldosterone release.
glossary.Aldosterone: Adrenal hormone that makes the kidney keep sodium and water and lose potassium.
glossary.Creatinine: A muscle waste product cleared by the kidneys; a rise means worse kidney function.
glossary.GFR: Glomerular filtration rate: how much blood the kidneys filter each minute.
glossary.Aldosterone antagonist: Drug that blocks aldosterone's receptor, such as spironolactone.
glossary.Adrenal medulla: The inner part of the adrenal gland that makes adrenaline and noradrenaline.
glossary.Catecholamines: Adrenaline, noradrenaline and dopamine: the 'fight or flight' hormones.
glossary.Adrenaline: A hormone that raises heart rate, BP and sweating; also called epinephrine.
glossary.Noradrenaline: A hormone and neurotransmitter that tightens blood vessels; also called norepinephrine.
glossary.Adrenergic: Relating to adrenaline's receptors (alpha and beta).
glossary.Diuretic: A drug that makes the kidneys pass more salt and water.
